cells.note: The study synthesized descriptions from the literature through qualitative content analysis; this is a reported qualitative contrast, not a pooled experimental effect.

cells.quote: VPs “can cater to a large number of learners simultaneously and be used by learners repeatedly when needed” [44] “to reach more learners, at more times, in a wider geographic area, than they are able to do through face-to-face contact” [45].
cells.note: The study synthesized qualitative descriptions and reports the stated accessibility and scalability advantages of VPs.

O.outcome_detail: Standardization and flexibility of the learning experience

cells.quote: Compared to bedside teaching or teaching with standardized patients (SPs), “virtual patients offer true standardization across interactions creating a more consistent but less flexible experience for learners” [53].
cells.note: The direction is mixed because VPs are described as better for consistency/standardization but worse for flexibility.

D.treatment: VPs described as widely or increasingly adopted
D.comparison: VPs described as not yet widely adopted or having lower-than-expected adoption

O.outcome_detail: Adoption of virtual patients in healthcare education

cells.quote: Opinions varied about whether VPs are well adopted, an upcoming activity or not (yet) well adopted in healthcare education. Statements ranged from “resulting in lower adoption rates than might be expected” [54], “growth in the use of virtual patients is likely to continue” [39], “VP technology is increasingly used” [55], to VPs are “widely adopted” [56].
cells.note: This is a qualitative synthesis of descriptions in the literature, not a comparative intervention study; the reported adoption claims vary across sources.
